title: Application to vacate stay of execution of sentence of death

pages.text:
No. ----------
 
In the Supreme Court of the United States
CAPITAL CASE
EXECUTION SCHEDULED:SEPTEMBER 30,2026, AT 10:00AM(CDT)
KENNETH NELSEN,WARDEN, 
APPLICANT
v.
CHRISTA PIKE,
RESPONDENT
APPLICATION TO VACATE STAY 
OF EXECUTION OF DEATH SENTENCE
Jonathan Skrmetti
Attorney General & Reporter
Madeline W. Clark
Solicitor General
John Bledsoe
Deputy Attorney General
Counsel of Record
OFFICE OF THE TENNESSEE 
ATTORNEY GENERAL 
P.O. Box 20207
Nashville, TN 37202
(615) 741-4351
John.Bledsoe@ag.tn.gov

1
To the Honorable Brett M. Kavanaugh, Associate Justice of the Supreme Court 
of the United States and Circuit Justice for the Sixth Circuit:
Applicant Kenneth Nelsen, Warden, respectfully requests that the Court 
vacate the stay of execution entered by a divided panel of the Sixth Circuit. In re Pike, 
No. 26-5864 (6th Cir., Order, Sept. 30, 2026); Order, D.10.1 Respondent Pike is a 
Tennessee inmate scheduled for execution by lethal injection today at 10:00 a.m. 
(CDT), for the brutal murder of nineteen-year-old Colleen Slemmer. The Sixth 
Circuit’s order—entered less than two hours before Pike’s scheduled execution—
blocks the State’s enforcement of a thirty-year-old criminal judgment for the sole 
purpose of the Court to consider whether Pike’s Rule 60(b) motion for relief from 
judgment is properly considered a second or successive habeas petition. 
This Court should vacate the stay. The Sixth Circuit granted a stay—that Pike 
did not even request—without determining that Pike is likely to succeed on the merits 
and without addressing the last-minute nature of her Rule 60(b) motion. “Even if the 
Sixth Circuit believed that the . . . issue was difficult, that belief still would not have 
been a sufficient reason to grant a stay. Under the traditional stay factors, a 
petitioner is required to make a strong showing that he is likely to succeed on the 
merits.” Price v. Dunn, 587 U.S. 999, 1004-05 (2019) (cleaned up). And Pike is not
likely to succeed on the merits because, as Judge Griffin explained in dissent, Pike’s 
Rule 60(b) motion is a second and successive habeas petition in disguise that presses 
1 Citations are to the docket entries in the Sixth Circuit are to D. and the docket 
entry number.

2
a claim she already unsuccessfully presented. See Gonzalez v. Crosby, 545 U.S. 524, 
532 (2005).
Pike filed her Rule 60(b) motion yesterday, even though the basis for her 
motion arose more than a month ago. This type of gamesmanship is familiar in 
capital litigation. See, e.g., Price, 587 U.S. at 1008 (Thomas, J., concurring in denial 
of certiorari). But here, the Sixth Circuit rewarded it. The State’s strong interest in 
finality and the surviving victims’ right to closure require rejection of Pike’s attempt 
“to interpose unjustified delay.” Bucklew v. Precythe, 587 U.S. 119, 150 (2019). As 
Colleen’s mother recently said, “Thirty-one years is long enough.” This Court should 
vacate the stay.
BACKGROUND
On January 12, 1995, Christa Pike beat, tortured, and killed Colleen Slemmer 
because Pike “just felt mean that day.” State v. Pike, 978 S.W.2d 904, 908 (Tenn. 
1998). Pike cut Colleen’s throat six times, struck her in the back with a meat cleaver, 
and crushed her skull with a piece of asphalt. Id. at 910-11. A jury convicted Pike of 
first-degree murder based on overwhelming evidence of guilt, including a detailed 
confession, and sentenced her to death on the strength of multiple aggravating 
factors. Id. at 910, 912, 914. The Tennessee Supreme Court affirmed Pike’s 
convictions and sentence in 1998. Id. at 914. 
Pike then unsuccessfully sought state post-conviction relief. Pike v. State, No. 
E2009-00016-CCA-R3-PD, 2011 WL 1544207 (Tenn. Crim. App. Apr. 25, 2011), perm. 
app. denied (Tenn. Nov. 15, 2011). The post-conviction court rejected her contention

3
that her trial counsel were ineffective for failing to investigate and present additional 
mitigating evidence of her childhood, including sexual abuse, at sentencing. Order, 
R.9-5, 4435-39, 4463-77.2 The post-conviction court did so on grounds that have 
nothing to do with the credibility of Pike’s abuse allegations. The court held that “the 
jury’s verdict would not have been affected by the mitigating evidence now offered 
due to the strength of the facts of this case for guilt and the strength of the 
aggravating factors.” Id., 4477. The court explained that “[e]ven assuming that all 
the evidence” Pike presented on post-conviction review “had been presented to the 
jury,” it could not “find that the jury’s sentencing verdict would have been any 
different.” Id. The court further determined that much of Pike’s additional evidence 
was cumulative of evidence her counsel presented and that some of it “would have 
included some very negative information about the petitioner” or opened the door to 
damaging rebuttal. Id. 
The Tennessee Court of Criminal Appeals affirmed on exactly these grounds, 
holding that “based upon the clear finding by the trial court that the mitigation 
evidence which was omitted would not have outweighed the aggravating factors, the 
Petitioner is essentially precluded from establishing prejudice.” Pike, 2011 WL 
1544207, at *52. 
Applying the deferential review applicable under 28 U.S.C. § 2254(d) to the 
state-court adjudication, the federal district court rejected Pike’s ineffective2 Record citations, referenced as R., are to the docket entries in the district court. See 
Pike v. Freeman, No. 1:12-cv-00035 (E.D. Tenn.).

4
assistance claim related to mitigation when denying Pike’s habeas petition. Pike v. 
Freeman, No. 1:12-cv-00035, 2016 WL 1050717, at *11-16 (E.D. Tenn. Mar. 11, 2016). 
On appeal, the Sixth Circuit affirmed the denial of federal habeas relief, noting 
that “none of the evidence Pike now points to substantially differs from the mitigation 
case that was presented to the jury.” Pike v. Gross, 936 F.3d 372, 379-82 (6th Cir. 
2019). Even if the jury had heard everything Pike now says it should have, “the sheer 
weight and degree of aggravation evidence before the jury outweighs the mitigation 
evidence,” because her proffered evidence was “mostly cumulative and insufficient to 
overcome the heinous nature of her crime.” Id. at 383.
On September 30, 2025, the Tennessee Supreme Court set Pike’s execution for 
September 30, 2026. Order, State v. Pike, No. M2020-01156-SC-DPE-DD (Tenn. Sept. 
30, 2025).3 
On June 12, 2026, Pike filed a motion with the Tennessee Supreme Court, 
asserting facial and as-applied challenges to Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol and 
requesting the appointment of a special master “to develop the facts to support these 
claims.” Order, State v. Pike, No. M2020-01156-SC-DPE-DD (Sept. 23, 2026). Citing 
a history of rape and sexual abuse, Pike argued that placing her, “as the lone female 
in a vulnerable position surrounded by male corrections officers during the last days 
of her life will trigger her PTSD and result in a torturous execution or mental 
decompensation to the point she will be incompetent to be executed.” Motion, State 
3 This order, as well as subsequent filings related to Pike’s attempt to stay the order, 
are publicly available at https://pch.tncourts.gov/.

5
v. Pike, No. M2020-01156-SC-DPE-DD (Tenn. Jun. 12, 2026). The Tennessee 
Supreme Court appointed a special master to conduct an evidentiary hearing and 
make findings on Pike’s claims relating to her mental struggles and sexual abuse. 
Order, State v. Pike, No. M2020-01156-SC-DPE-DD (Tenn. Jul. 10, 2026). 
At the August 13, 2026 hearing, during argument related to Pike’s mental 
health claims and sexual abuse, the State’s attorney stated:
“The State does not dispute the terrible things that Ms. Pike suffered. I 
think everybody in this courtroom wishes that those things had never 
happened to Ms. Pike. I think we all wish that we were not here today 
and that she was not on death row . . . . And so it’s certainly not the 
State’s intention to try to minimize the suffering that Ms. Pike has 
experienced.”
D.9-2, 82-83. 
The special master and the Tennessee Supreme Court ultimately rejected all 
of Pike’s claims. Order, State v. Pike, No. M2020-01156-SC-DPE-DD (Sept. 23, 2026). 
Pike then filed an application for stay of execution and petition for writ of certiorari, 
which this Court denied on September 29, 2026. Order, Pike v. Tennessee, Nos. 
26A414, 26-5696 (U.S. Sept. 29, 2026). 
Later that day—hours before her scheduled execution—Pike filed a motion for 
relief from judgment under Fed. R. Civ. P. 60(b). Motion, R.116. Relying on the 
State’s above August 2026 statement regarding purported abuse committed against 
Pike as a child, she sought to reopen her petition to relitigate the lower federal courts’ 
merits-rejection of her claim that trial counsel provided ineffective assistance at 
sentencing. In Pike’s view, the above-quoted characterization of her prior reports of

6
sexual abuse differs from that offered by the State on post-conviction review4 and 
qualified as extraordinary circumstances for reopening her concluded habeas petition 
and relitigating the merits of her mitigation-related ineffective-assistance clam.5
The State filed a motion to transfer Pike’s motion to the Sixth Circuit, as a 
second or successive habeas corpus petition. Motion, R.118. By order filed September 
29, 2026, the district court granted the State’s motion and transferred Pike’s motion 
to the Sixth Circuit as a second or successive habeas petition. Order, R.119. Pike 
filed a motion to remand. 
Although Pike did not ask for a stay of execution, a divided panel of the Sixth 
Circuit—at 8:17 a.m. CDT on September 30, 2026—granted a “short stay of execution 
in order to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments and resolve the 
issues on the merits,” without analyzing all the relevant factors for granting a stay of 
execution. D.10-2.
Judge Griffin dissented. D.10-2, 4-7. As he explained, Pike’s claim fails under 
28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(1) because she asserts “a claim . . . that was presented in a prior 
application” for habeas corpus relief—“the ineffective assistance of counsel at the 
sentencing stage.” Id., 6. At bottom, Pike’s “claim is that the State’s recent remarks 
undermine the state court’s prejudice determinations.” Id. But “[w]hether the state 
4 Pike did not testify at the evidentiary hearings on her post-conviction petition conducted in 2007 
and 2008, nor did she testify at the more recent hearing on her stay motion. Instead, other witnesses 
testified in those proceedings about Pike’s reports of abuse.
5 On September 28, 2026, Pike moved the Tennessee Supreme Court to recall the 2011 mandate in 
her state post-conviction appeal on essentially the same grounds. That motion was denied. Order, 
Pike v. State, No. E2009-00016-SC-R11-PD (Tenn. Sept. 29, 2026).

7
court’s application of federal law or view of the facts was unreasonable was the whole 
merits decision.” Id. And when a Rule 60(b) motion “attacks the federal court’s 
previous resolution of a claim on the merits,” it is subject to the procedural bar on 
second or successive petitions. Gonzalez v. Crosby, 545 U.S. 524, 532 
(2005). Accordingly, Judge Griffin would “deny Pike’s Motion to Remand and dismiss 
Pike’s second or successive application pursuant to AEDPA.” D.10-2, 6.
REASONS FOR VACATING THE STAY OF EXECUTION
This Court has long concluded that a stay of execution is an equitable remedy, 
and that “equity must be sensitive to the State’s strong interest in enforcing its 
criminal judgments without undue interference from the federal courts.” Hill, 547 
U.S. at 584. Indeed, “[b]oth the State and the victims of crime have an important 
interest in the timely enforcement of a sentence.” Id. For this reason, even for a 
“short stay,” a stay of execution requires “a showing of a significant possibility of 
success on the merits.” Id. 
“A court considering a stay must also apply ‘a strong equitable presumption 
against the grant of a stay where a claim could have been brought at such a time as 
to allow consideration of the merits without requiring entry of a stay.’” Id. (quoting 
Nelson, 541 U.S. at 650). “If litigation is allowed to proceed, federal courts can and 
should protect settled state judgments from undue interference by invoking their 
equitable powers to dismiss or curtail suits that are pursued in a dilatory fashion or 
based on speculative theories.” Bucklew, 587 U.S. at 150-51.

8
The Sixth Circuit should not have granted a stay here, as Judge Griffin’s 
dissent explains. Upon a proper weighing of the relevant factors, Pike is not entitled
to a stay of execution.
A. Pike is not likely to succeed on her motion for relief from judgment.
To start, Pike is not likely to succeed in the ultimate resolution of her Rule 
60(b) motion because her motion is nothing more than an attempt to relitigate the 
merits of her rejected mitigation-related ineffective-assistance claim. Nothing 
supports a stay of execution—“short” or otherwise—because Pike’s construed second 
or successive petition is barred by 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(1). The State can show a 
likelihood of success in that review. 
Gonzalez v. Crosby, 545 U.S. 524 (2005), clearly disallows Pike’s effort to 
smuggle a second or successive petition into a motion for relief from judgment. It is 
blackletter law that a motion for relief from judgment in a habeas case that “attacks 
the federal court’s previous resolution of a claim on the merits” “impermissibly 
circumvent[s]” statutory limitations on second or successive habeas petitions. Id. at 
532 (citing 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(3)) (emphasis in original). Try as she might to show 
otherwise, this describes Pike’s motion to a T. Her Rule 60(b) motion is not a 
challenge to “some defect in the integrity of the federal habeas proceedings.” Id. It 
is a request for relitigation of a federal claim on the merits based upon what she 
believes to be new evidence—a supposed “concession” by the State. Motion, R.116, 
13534. That is not the proper subject of a Rule 60(b) motion.

9
And this purported concession is not even new evidence; it has no relationship 
to the ineffectiveness claim previously rejected. Pike claims that a sympathetic 
statement made by counsel for the State in a state-court hearing on her stay motion 
conceded instances of childhood abuse that she reported during state post-conviction 
review, purportedly contrary to arguments advanced by the State on collateral 
review. She suggests that but-for the State’s skepticism of her credibility, the state 
post-conviction court would have accepted her claim that her counsel was ineffective 
for failing to present mitigation evidence of childhood abuse at sentencing. The state 
court, however, rejected Pike’s claim for reasons that have nothing to do with Pike’s 
credibility or the veracity of her allegations regarding childhood abuse. The federal 
courts on habeas review likewise rejected Pike’s claims on a different basis. Any 
statements made by the State regarding Pike’s credibility have no relevance to the 
basis for the denial of her claim.
Even assuming the State made some sort of concession in the recent 
evidentiary hearing, there too the State’s view of Pike’s childhood abuse played no 
role in the consideration of the claims she raised at that hearing. As reflected in a 
full review of counsel’s closing arguments, the State advocated that Pike was not 
entitled to a stay of execution notwithstanding evidence presented on her allegations 
of childhood abuse. D.9-2. That argument is entirely consistent with the basis for 
the earlier denials of Pike’s mitigation-related ineffective-assistance claim by both 
the federal district court and the Sixth Circuit.

10
In short, Pike’s Rule 60(b) motion is a second or successive motion in disguise, 
and regardless, the State’s expression of sympathy in the face of Pike’s unsupported 
stay request created no “extraordinary circumstance” for successive habeas review on 
a claim previously rejected upon full merits review. Pike’s remanded request for postjudgment relief will ultimately prove unsuccessful and her claim is not certworthy. 
Both weigh mightily in favor of vacating the stay of execution.
B. The Remaining Stay Factors Compel a Vacatur of the Stay of 
Execution.
Pike’s abusive, tactical delay is reason enough to vacate the stay. “[T]he lastminute nature of an application that could have been brought earlier, or an 
applicant’s attempt at manipulation, may be grounds for denial of a stay.” Bucklew, 
587 U.S. at 150 (cleaned up). It is well known that “capital petitioners might 
deliberately engage in dilatory tactics to prolong their incarceration and avoid 
execution of a sentence of death.” Rhines v. Weber, 544 U.S. 269, 277-78 (2005). “[I]t 
is the same strategy adopted by many death-row inmates with an impending 
execution: bring last-minute claims that will delay the execution, no matter how 
groundless.” Price v. Dunn, 587 U.S. 999, 1008 (2019) (Thomas, J., concurring in 
denial of certiorari). Federal courts accordingly apply “a strong equitable 
presumption against the grant of a stay where a claim could have been brought at 
such a time as to allow consideration of the merits without requiring entry of a stay.” 
Nelson v. Campbell, 541 U.S. 637, 650 (2004).
That presumption should foreclose a stay here when Pike waited 47 days after 
the so-called “concession,” until the eve of her schedule execution date, to seek relief

11
from her judgment. She could have more promptly sought post-judgment relief in the 
preceding 47 days. Yet she waited until the very last possible moment to seek relief 
under Rule 60(b) and further delay justice. And it worked: The Sixth Circuit granted 
a stay to give it time to consider her arguments. “The proper response to this 
maneuvering is to deny [her] meritless request[] expeditiously” and vacate the stay. 
Price, 587 U.S. at 1008.
Importantly, the harm a stay causes Colleen Slemmer’s family weighs heavily 
in favor of vacatur. The State and crime victims have a “powerful and legitimate 
interest in punishing the guilty.” Calderon v. Thompson, 523 U.S. 538, 556 (1998) 
(cleaned up). They also “have an important interest in the timely enforcement of a 
[death] sentence.” Bucklew, 587 U.S. at 149 (cleaned up); see Tenn. Const. art. I, §35 
(providing constitutional right to crime victims). “Only with an assurance of real 
finality can the State execute its moral judgment in a case” and “the victims of crime 
move forward knowing the moral judgment will be carried out.” Calderon, 523 U.S. 
at 556. “To unsettle these expectations is to inflict a profound injury.” Id.
That injury is very real for Colleen’s family. Slemmer’s mother and stepfather, 
May and Raul Martinez, have traveled to Tennessee for Pike’s execution. Anthony 
Austin, Colleen Slemmer’s family heads to Tennessee ahead of Christa Pike’s 
execution, First Coast News (Sept. 28, 2026), https://tinyurl.com/yw2p9nyt. For her 
mother, “Pike’s conviction and sentencing were only the beginning of a decades-long 
nightmare.” Steven Hale, Tennessee Prepares to Execute Christa Pike for the Murder 
of Colleen Slemmer, Nashville Banner (Sept. 14, 2026), https://perma.cc/LK4T-LFP2.

12
She recently explained that “she hoped witnessing the execution herself would quiet 
a fear of Pike that has stayed with her for decades.” Id. And her stepfather explained 
that he “just want[s] to see it happen” because “[t]hat’ll be the final chapter of this 
case closed.” Anthony Austin, 31 Years of Fighting: Colleen Slemmer’s parents say 
they’ll skip mortgage to watch her killer die, First Coast News, (Sept. 3, 2026), 
https://tinyurl.com/3u5fccry. May Martinez put it best: “Thirty-one years is long 
enough to wait.” Keith Sharon, Remembering Colleen Slemmer, the teenager killed 
by Christa Pike, The Tennessean (Sept. 28, 2026), https://perma.cc/R9LZ-BVEN. It 
is far past time for Colleen’s family to receive the closure they seek. 
The public interest further tips the balance against a stay and in favor of a 
vacatur. Thirty-one “years after [Pike’s] capital sentence . . . both the state and the 
public have an interest in finality which, if not deserving of respect yet, may never 
receive respect.” Workman v. Bell, 484 F.3d 837, 842 (6th Cir. 2007).
The Court should vacate the stay of execution to avoid rewarding Pike’s 
abusive delay tactics, to prevent further trauma to Colleen’s family, and to protect 
Tennessee’s grave sovereign interest in the execution of its exhaustively reviewed 
judgment.

13
Respectfully submitted,
Jonathan Skrmetti
Attorney General & Reporter
Madeline W. Clark
Solicitor General
